cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Tensile strength is the maximum stress a material can withstand while being stretched before it breaks.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Toughness is the ability of a material to absorb energy and deform plastically before fracturing; tough materials resist impact.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Brittleness is the tendency to fracture with little or no plastic deformation; brittle materials fail suddenly (e.g. cast iron, ceramics).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into a wire; ductile materials undergo significant plastic deformation before breaking (e.g. copper, low-carbon steel).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Malleability is the ability to be shaped by hammering or pressing; malleable materials deform under compression without cracking (e.g. lead, aluminium).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Hardness is the resistance to surface indentation, scratching or wear; hard materials resist deformation (e.g. hardened steel, ceramics).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Stiffness (Young's Modulus) is resistance to elastic deformation; stiff materials deflect little under load (e.g. steel, CFRP).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Density is mass per unit volume; low-density materials (aluminium, polymers) are chosen where weight matters.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Material selection considers: required properties, operating conditions (temperature, corrosion), cost, availability, manufacturability and sustainability.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Stress = Force / Area (units: N/mm2 or MPa); Strain = Change in length / Original length (dimensionless).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: A factor of safety is applied: FoS = Ultimate tensile strength / Working stress; typical values range from 2 to 10 depending on the application.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Material Properties & Selection
cards.back: Properties can be altered by processing: heat treatment, cold working, alloying and reinforcing all modify material behaviour.

cards.front: What should you know about gcse engineering exam tips — material properties & selection?
cards.back: 1. For Material Properties & Selection questions, use precise design and technology terminology 2. Consider function, aesthetics, ergonomics, sustainability and cost in your answers 3. When evaluating, justify your design decisions with reference to user needs and specifications 4. Show your understanding of Material Properties & Selection through both theory and practical application 5. Reference real products and manufacturing processes where relevant
